source_title: Before the election, Netanyahu offered a grim economic forecast for Israel.
source_excerpt:
David M. Halbfinger Max Bearak Isabel Kershner Aaron Boxerman and Johnatan Reiss
Israelis voted in the largest numbers in a generation on Tuesday, and exit polls suggested that a bloc of opposition parties was roughly even with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s alliance in what many described as a make-or-break moment for the nation.
The election did not appear to immediately determine who would lead the country next, even as the leading candidates — Mr. Netanyahu and the leader of a coalition of opposition parties, Gadi Eisenkot — struck tones of victory in late-night addresses to supporters. Vote counting was expected to last days, followed by a potentially lengthy effort by the blocs to assemble a parliamentary majority.
The exit polls, if accurate, suggest that neither Mr. Netanyahu’s bloc nor the one led by Mr. Eisenkot , a former military chief whose son was killed in the Gaza war, will be able to form a government without relying on two Arab parties that were projected to win as many as 17 or 18 seats in Parliament. Mr. Netanyahu effectively ruled out including them in a governing coalition, and Mr. Eisenkot and his partners have balked at the idea, too.
One option analysts are already weighing is whether Mr. Netanyahu, who has led the most far-right government in Israeli history, could join with Mr. Eisenkot or others in the opposition to form a unity government. But a unity government would face major obstacles, given how deeply Mr. Eisenkot’s voters despise Mr. Netanyahu, and because the two would have to agree on which of them would serve as prime minister. Mr. Netanyahu is unlikely to give up control, while Mr. Eisenkot has called the prime minister unfit to lead Israel.
Much remained unclear early Wednesday morning in Israel. Making matters even murkier, Israel’s exit polls have a spotty history of accuracy, particularly in tight races.
Mr. Eisenkot appeared onstage past midnight at his post-election party and attempted to strike a tone of triumph — as well as defiance toward Mr. Netanyahu.
“Tonight we got the answer: The public wants change,” he said.
Mr. Netanyahu addressed his supporters a few hours later, invoking his relationship with President Trump and repeating his pre-election talking points about removing the threat of Iran. He sounded triumphant, saying it was clear that Likud had emerged as the largest party in Israel and mocking months of pre-election polls that showed his party trailing behind that of Mr. Eisenkot.
“We must form a strong right-wing government,” he declared.
In the coming days, after official vote totals are released and parliamentary seats are allocated to parties, Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, will invite the party leader he thinks has the best chance to assemble a governing coalition. Such a coalition would usually have to be made up of at least 61 lawmakers, though Mr. Eisenkot has floated the idea of forming a minority government.
One factor not reflected in exit polls are the hundreds of thousands of votes cast by Israelis at special polling stations, including at military bases, hospitals, prisons and embassies. In the previous election, those votes tended to favor the coalition of Mr. Netanyahu and his allies.
Arab parties: The exit polls pointed to at least one surprise in projecting that two Arab parties would win as many as 17 or 18 seats in the 120-seat Parliament. That would be their strongest showing ever, and potentially give them an important role in forming the next government. Read more ›

War fears: Amid reports that Mr. Netanyahu has been pushing for renewed attacks on Iran, Mr. Eisenkot warned him in his speech to supporters not to abuse his power as caretaker prime minister to influence the process of forming a new government. “Netanyahu, don’t dare use Israel’s security for your political needs,” he said.
War fears: Amid reports that Mr. Netanyahu has been pushing for renewed attacks on Iran, Mr. Eisenkot warned him in his speech to supporters not to abuse his power as caretaker prime minister to influence the process of forming a new government. “Netanyahu, don’t dare use Israel’s security for your political needs,” he said.
It’s nearly 4 a.m. in Israel, and there is no clear winner. News is expected to slow down in the coming hours, but pick up again in the morning, when party leaders are expected to begin discussing potential alliances. The official results are still a long way off: Election authorities have so far counted nearly a million votes, about a fifth of the total votes cast.
In a nod to the fact he is now a caretaker prime minister pending the formation of a new government, Netanyahu said the exit polls were only a preview and he was waiting for official results. Yet he sounded triumphant, if not quite saying he had won the election. He said it was clear that his Likud party had emerged as the largest party in the Parliament, and he mocked months of pre-election polls that showed Likud trailing behind the party of his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot.
Four Ways Israel’s Election Could End. Eventually.
No party is expected to achieve a clear victory, which means the election will likely only be the first step in determining who will form the next government. Here’s how that might unfold.

Listing Israel’s enemies who have now been killed, including Ayatollah Ali Khamenei of Iran, Netanyahu declared, “Iran is weaker than ever, Israel is stronger than ever.”
“But it’s still not over,” he said, adding that with his “friend” President Trump, it would be possible to remove the threat from Iran once and for all, repeating his pre-election talking points.
Netanyahu showed no hint of extending a hand to the opposition as he addressed supporters early Wednesday. Arriving onstage at 3:15 a.m., looking reinvigorated and in an ebullient mood, he declared, “We must form a strong right-wing government.”
One updated exit poll has given Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc a small edge over the opposition. The exit polls by Israel’s three largest television networks at first projected a small lead for Gadi Eisenkot’s anti-Netanyahu alliance, but now one has Netanyahu and his allies ahead, and the other two show the two blocs even. Exit polls have not always been reliable indicators of the result, and the official count is far from complete. But it appears that neither side has a clear path to forming a government without the help of the Arab parties, unless one or more parties defects from one of the main blocs.
Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main rival, took the stage in the early hours of Wednesday morning like a winner, embracing members of his Yashar party who were waiting for him there and waving to an enthusiastic crowd of flag-waving supporters who hailed him as the next prime minister.
Although Eisenkot’s path to forming a government is far from clear, he gave what amounted to a victory speech for the opposition bloc, declaring, “We’ve made history.” Describing the election as a referendum on who should lead Israel in the coming years, he added: “Tonight we got the answer. The public wants change.”
In an unusual and pointed message, Eisenkot told the country’s security chiefs and public servants that Netanyahu now heads a transitional government that has lost the confidence of the people. “Stand strong and firm against any attempt to challenge you,” Eisenkot said. “You have my clear backing.” Amid reports that Netanyahu has been pushing for renewed attacks on Iran, Eisenkot said, “Netanyahu, don’t dare use Israel’s security for your political needs.”
Two Israeli news channels have recently updated their exit polls, which now show a tie between the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and that of his main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot. Neither bloc, however, has enough seats to form a government without the support of Arab parties. Earlier versions of the same exit polls had shown small leads for the opposition alliance. The official vote count is still too preliminary to draw any conclusions, and counting will take days.
Arab parties could play a role in forming the next government.
One of the most striking results from the election in Israel on Tuesday was the unusually strong showing by two leading Arab parties, whose voters turned out in record numbers to express their opposition to the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The final results have not been announced, but a range of exit polls conducted by Israeli broadcasters suggest that two of the parties — the socially conservative United Arab List, or Raam, and the left-wing Joint List — may have won a historically large number of seats in parliament and an important role in the formation of the country’s next government.
Mansour Abbas, the leader of Raam, told a television interviewer that the turnout showed that Arab voters, who make up about 20 percent of Israel’s population, had channeled their “frustration and despair” into “hope.”
He said he wanted to replace Mr. Netanyahu’s government “in every possible way” and that his first priority was to “ensure that there is a chance of forming a government” that achieved that goal.
The Arab parties’ strong showing may make them kingmakers. But building a governing coalition with Arab participation remains a fraught exercise in Israel. Many Israeli Jews believe that a parliamentary majority should not rely on the support of Arab lawmakers.
Most Arab citizens are the descendants of Palestinians who remained in their homes during the 1948 Arab-Israel war at the time of Israel’s independence.
Today, they mostly live in separate towns from Jewish Israelis and face violence and discriminatory housing policies.
Over the decades, disagreements, including over Israel’s nature as a Jewish state, have led many Arab voters to avoid the ballot box.
This week, many Arab voters said they were furious at Mr. Netanyahu for his treatment of the Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza and for policies that they feel treat Palestinians in Israel as second-class citizens. Indeed, throughout the campaign, Mr. Netanyahu made overt appeals to anti-Arab prejudice.
“I’m very optimistic because people understand that this isn’t like ordinary elections — we want change,” said Kholoud Al-Zeinati, 39, an Arab Israeli voter who cast her ballot on Tuesday in the mixed Jewish-Arab city of Lod, where long lines formed at polling places. “Because we, as the Arab community, are the community that pays the biggest price across so many aspects of life, it’s important to come out and take part.”
“I expect our votes to be truly decisive in shaping the next government and making things better for all of us,” she added.
Of the two Arab parties that did well on Tuesday, only Raam has joined a coalition government in the past. That happened in 2021, when it joined the short-lived anti-Netanyahu coalition of Prime Minister Naftali Bennett.
Raam’s participation in that government outraged many right-wing Jewish voters, and when it collapsed after roughly one year, they backed Mr. Netanyahu, who went on to form the most hard-line government in Israel’s history.
That government now faces the possibility that it may be brought down by an election result that has been deeply shaped by robust Arab turnout.
Heedo Abu Laban contributed reporting from Lod, Israel.
Scores of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s supporters and lawmakers from his Likud party are gathered at the party’s election-night headquarters, in a conference hall in Jerusalem. It’s past 1:30 a.m., and some of the crowd here is ecstatic, waiting for the prime minister to come and speak onstage. Activists are wearing “Make Israel Great Again” baseball hats and throwing the party’s voting slips like confetti. But others, including party officials, acknowledged to me their path to forming a coalition is narrow, and feelings here are mixed.
Bezalel Smotrich, the current finance minister and leader of the far-right Religious Zionism party, focused his post-election speech on delegitimizing the predominantly Arab parties whose support could help the anti-Netanyahu bloc form a government. “Parties that are unable to condemn the massacre of Oct. 7 and are not willing to declare Hamas as a terrorist organization are not legitimate actors in Israeli politics,” Smotrich told his supporters.
Naftali Bennett, who leads a party in the alliance opposing Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc, said the sitting prime minister had lost the election. In a fiery televised address to a gathering of supporters, he tied Netanyahu to the Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, Israel’s worst security failure in decades. “The government of Oct. 7 will go home,” he said.
He said the anti-Netanyahu parties “will do everything, setting ego aside” to form a government that will insist on conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews into the military. He did not address whether that might include Netanyahu’s Likud party, or one or more Arab parties.
Not reflected in exit polls are hundreds of thousands of ballots cast at special polling stations, including on military bases, in hospitals, prisons, and embassies. In the previous election, those votes leaned toward Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition. This year, the election authorities estimated that roughly 600,000 such votes would be cast, accounting for about 10 percent of eligible voters. Results from those ballots are not expected to be announced before Thursday.
Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right national security minister, was the first leader of a party in Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition to speak following tonight’s exit polls. He neither declared victory for his bloc nor conceded defeat. “The night is still young,” he told supporters at a televised gathering. He said he hoped that the bloc led by Netanyahu “was close to forming a right-wing government.”
The leader of the Democrats party, Yair Golan, declared victory on Tuesday night for the opposition bloc, which includes his party, and asserted that the exit polls showed that the Israeli public had “fired Netanyahu and Likud.” Addressing supporters, Golan urged opposition leaders to swiftly form a “change government” without letting ego or political calculations delay the process. “From tonight, Israel can breathe,” he said. “Tomorrow, we begin rebuilding.” He expressed a willingness to rely on support from outside the opposition alliance to secure a parliamentary majority, an apparent reference to the Arab parties.
Another surprise in the exit polls was Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s apparent surge on Election Day. While the most recent pre-election surveys showed his Likud party with about 20 seats in Parliament, the exit polls show Likud winning 24, more than any other party. That is an important symbolic victory for Netanyahu, and one that few could have foreseen for the prime minister who was in charge on Oct. 7, 2023.
It suggests that Netanyahu’s hair-on-fire appeal to voters on Election Day worked — but only so much. The extra four seats he picked up, according to the exit polls, came at the expense of his allies, not the opposition bloc.
Judging by exit polls, one major suprise in this election is the high turnout among Israel’s Arab citizens, who were furious at the current government over its housing policies and its failure to curb violent crime in Arab communities.
Pre-election surveys suggested that the two main Arab parties would win about 13 seats, but the exit polls suggest they will end up with closer to 17 or 18 seats. In the past, Arab parties have never won more than 15.
Mansour Abbas, the leader of the Raam party, told a television interviewer on Tuesday night that the turnout showed that “frustration and despair” in Israel’s Arab society had “turned to hope.”
Mansour Abbas, the leader of an Arab party that could prove pivotal to the opposition’s efforts to form a majority coalition, said he wanted to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government “in every possible way.” In an interview with Israel’s Channel 12, he said his immediate priority was to “ensure that there is a chance of forming a government” opposed to Netanyahu. “And then, we will discuss the details,” he said, “and address the challenges.”
Initial exit polls suggest that Arab parties are likely to win a historic number of seats in Israel’s Parliament.
The polls released by Israeli TV channels gave Raam and the Joint List, the two major Arab parties, either 17 or 18 of the Knesset’s 120 seats.
“The Arabs feel this government did everything to marginalize them and even incite against them,” said Thabet Abu Ras, an expert in Arab-Jewish relations and an Arab citizen of Israel. “They understood they needed to fight for their citizenship and play the political game fully.”
Israel’s Central Election Committee just updated the country’s turnout rate to 77.7 percent, the highest since 1999. Israelis headed in large numbers to the polls on Tuesday, particularly among the country’s Arab minority, who were spurred by a desire to unseat Benjamin Netanyahu’s hardline coalition.
In 2021, Israel’s short-lived anti-Netanyahu government included for the first time an independent Arab party, Raam. The backlash to that catapulted anti-Arab politicians like Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich into the next government. According to exit polls, the backlash to that government appears to have resulted today in a record showing for Israel’s Arab parties.
The exit polls suggest Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition may well be deadlocked with his Jewish opponents, and neither would be able to form a government on their own without relying on Arab parties. One option already being weighed by analysts is whether Netanyahu and his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, could form a unity government of Israel’s right-wing and centrist parties. Such an alliance might be hard for Eisenkot to accept given how deeply his own voters despise Netanyahu. And then there’s also the question of who would run the government. Netanyahu is unlikely to give up control, and Eisenkot has vowed not to join a government run by someone he has called unfit to lead Israel.
There have been precedents in the past where the party with the most seats in Parliament does not end up forming a government. In Israel’s 2009 election, Tzipi Livni’s centrist Kadima party won 28 seats, narrowly beating Benjamin Netanyahu’s conservative Likud, which won 27. But Netanyahu had more support from allied parties and came back as prime minister after a decade spent out of politics or in the opposition.
A few activists were celebrating at the Likud Party’s election headquarters in Jerusalem even though most exit polls suggested that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s alliance of parties had won fewer seats than the bloc of parties seeking his ouster. “Bibi is the king! The king is Bibi!” they shouted, using a nickname for the Israeli leader.
What to expect now that the polls have closed in Israel.
Polls have closed in Israel, and initial exit polls by Israeli broadcasters are expected to be released shortly afterward. But it will be hours before the definitive results are known, and it could be weeks until a new government is formed.

Twice before, Netanyahu was ousted then returned to power.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing coalition has the distinction of surviving for a full four-year term in office, something no government in Israel has achieved for more than 30 years. Since first taking office in 1996, he has tallied 19 years in power and become Israel’s longest-serving prime minister by far.
On Tuesday, he is seeking a seventh term, in Israel’s first parliamentary election since the deadly Hamas-led attack in 2023 that prompted its devastating war in Gaza.
The longevity of his most recent governing coalition followed three years during which a cycle of collapsed coalitions and five snap elections
